messages.subject: Huge C.I. ranges
parts:
Hello,

I have been working with some data which was collected last year over a 3 day period with sampling in the day and evening. 3 transects were thus sampled 6 times each.

According to the histograms the data seems to be fine, especially in the cases where I use size as a factor or use binning; but once I go into the summary section I am seeing rather large abundance and density estimates, and the lcl and ucl are ranging across a massive scale (from 2012.759 to 511015.9 for example). 

I have tried to include cluster size, daytime, habitat as factors in the models, have tried to test if anything would change if I only included the smaller cluster sizes, tried it with and without binning, with and without truncation, but nothing has lead to any real improvement. 

Attached is the data set I have been working on...if anyone could take a look and let me know what they think I would greatly appreciate it.

Thanks

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Huge C.I. ranges
parts:
Steve

Without looking at your data, I suspect the main challenge to producing precise estimates of abundance is your small number of transects.  You have but three transects, whereas general guidance is to have something on the order of 15-20. 

Variability in your abundance estimate is a combination of uncertainty in your detection function and uncertainty in encounter rate.  The main contributor to uncertainty in line transect estimates is encounter rate variance.  With only three transects you have a very poor estimate of that encounter rate variability.  All of the explorations you describe in your second paragraph may reduce some uncertainty in your detection function, but that uncertainty is usually small relative to the uncertainty in encounter rate.

Improving precision in your estimate will likely only result from an improved design in your survey with greater emphasis placed upon estimating encounter rate variability; via increased numbers of transects.
